```{r a6-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", out.width = "100%")
options(width = 82)
```

A `postrank()` result stores the assigned integer grades, the ordered and
unordered pair counts, the posterior expected loss, and the solver's status,
lower bound, and gap. When you export a table or report, keep those policy
settings and solver records alongside the grades so a reader knows what loss
was minimized and whether the solver finished within tolerance.

Below we load the two stored tutorial results introduced in
[Getting started: grading with one or two criteria](a1-getting-started.html)
using `postrank_example()`. Reading stored results runs no solver and fits no
model; the same accessors and export functions work on any `postrank_analysis`
returned by `postrank()`.

```{r a6-load}
library(postrank)
sites <- pr_tutorial
one <- postrank_example("tutorial_one")
two <- postrank_example("tutorial_two")
```

## Console output and `summary()` {#read-the-result-before-taking-a-column}

```{r a6-print}
print(one)
```

Printing `one` shows the entity and grade counts (`6 entities in 3 grades`),
the posterior loss (`0.0417`), the ordered ("disclosed", `12`) and unordered
("withheld", `3`) pair counts, the solver status and gap, and any warnings.
Grade 1 is the highest priority, and sharing a grade leaves that pair
unordered without claiming that the two sites have equal scores; see
[Getting started: grading with one or two criteria](a1-getting-started.html).

```{r a6-summary}
summary(one)
```

`summary(one)` adds the policy settings (`weights`, `G_max`, and `tau`), a
per-criterion table, the availability of optional summaries, and the full text
of recorded warnings. Under `Optional results:`, `"unsupported for this input"`
(here for Monte Carlo fragility, which was requested by default yet requires
posterior draws rather than an analytic normal distribution) is distinct from
`"not requested"` (meaning `FALSE` was passed before checking input support:
`crossfit = TRUE` also requires joint draws, whereas `diagnostics = TRUE` on a
normal input evaluates conditional-normal summaries under the `"Monte Carlo
diagnostics"` label). Neither label means a value of zero, and `summary()` never
runs new calculations.

On joint IID or MCMC draw inputs, `postrank()` computes pairwise Monte Carlo
fragility by default while leaving cross-fitting and full trace diagnostics off
unless requested. We can inspect `extras` and `fragility$summary` on the stored
30-site, three-criterion draw analysis (`analysis_30x3_tau35`):

```{r a6-extras}
a35 <- postrank_example("analysis_30x3_tau35")
do.call(rbind, lapply(a35[["extras"]], function(e) {
  data.frame(requested = e[["requested"]], available = e[["available"]],
    reason = if (is.null(e[["reason"]])) "" else e[["reason"]])
}))
a35[["fragility"]][["summary"]][c("pairs", "traced", "fragile",
  "fragile_disclosed", "fragile_tied")]
```

A pair is flagged as fragile when its estimated weighted error in the likelier
direction is within `z = 2` Monte Carlo standard errors of `tau`; these pairwise
flags are descriptive summaries of simulation noise and need not change the
jointly chosen grades (when `diagnostics = TRUE` or `crossfit = TRUE`, inspect
`x$diagnostics` and `x$crossfit`; see
[Monte Carlo diagnostics, cross-fitting, and IID bounds](m6-uncertainty-diagnostics.html)).

To add input and problem identity hashes, package and solver versions, and
source descriptions to the console summary, set `details = TRUE`. To capture the
formatted console lines as a character vector (matching the exported
`format_postrank_*_cli()` wrappers), call `format()`:

```{r a6-details}
detailed <- summary(one, details = TRUE)
head(format(one, width = 72, tier = 2), 4)
```

Printing `detailed` displays those extra provenance lines (including the note
`"Bounds are solver values; the gap is not regret"`, where regret means excess
loss relative to the best grading under the true posterior), and
`cat(..., sep = "\n")` writes captured `format()` lines to a log or file. In
scripts, extract numbers with the accessors below rather than parsing printed
console text.

## Grade tables and report-card tables {#take-a-stable-grade-table}

```{r a6-basic-table}
grade_table <- as.data.frame(one)
grade_table
```

By default, `as.data.frame()` returns a two-column data frame with character
`entity_id` and integer `grade` in the original input entity order. Calling
`as.data.frame()` on a `postrank_analysis`, its `postrank_fit`, or a
`postrank_baseline` always returns these same two columns, whether or not a
report card was prepared:

```{r a6-table-checks}
identical(grade_table$entity_id, sites$one$entity_ids)
identical(grade_table, as.data.frame(one$fit))
```

Join results back to your own entity metadata by `entity_id` rather than by
row position or formatted display labels.

To extract the marginal posterior summaries alongside the grades, request
`what = "report_card"`:

```{r a6-card-table}
card <- as.data.frame(one, what = "report_card")
names(card)
knitr::kable(card[, c("entity_id", "grade", "mean_score_A",
  "lower_score_A", "upper_score_A")], digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Entity", "Grade", "Mean", "Interval lower", "Interval upper"))
```

Along with `entity_id` and `grade`, `card` includes `sort_rank`, pair counts
for each entity (`n_above`, `n_below`, and `n_withheld`), and per-criterion
columns `mean_<criterion>`, `lower_<criterion>`, `upper_<criterion>`, and
`expected_rank_<criterion>` (here 90% equal-tail marginal score intervals).
If a criterion was negated at input construction (`orientation = "lower"`),
these columns remain on that negated scale, so negating back to raw units swaps
`lower_<criterion>` and `upper_<criterion>`. Select columns by name rather than
column index. When a marginal posterior is skewed, its posterior mean can sit
outside its equal-tail interval, and report-card tables and plots show the
stored values unchanged; likewise, inputs that carry precomputed intervals only
at one level (such as 90% in `pr_case_cde` and `pr_case_krw`, or 95% in
`pr_case_alabama`) cannot recompute other interval levels.

Rows of `as.data.frame(x, what = "report_card")` are ordered by `grade` and
then by the report card's secondary sort rule (`sort_rank`), which can differ
from the original input order:

```{r a6-order}
list(
  input_order = as.data.frame(two)$entity_id,
  report_card_order = as.data.frame(two, what = "report_card")$entity_id
)
```

If a report card could not be built (for example, when an input supplies
pairwise comparison probabilities without marginal intervals), calling
`as.data.frame(x, what = "report_card")` stops with an error explaining why it
is unavailable, while `as.data.frame(x)` still returns the two-column grade
table.

## Extracting grades, pair relations, profiles, and loss {#extract-grades-pair-relations-and-loss}

```{r a6-accessors}
grades <- get_grades(one)
grades
relations <- get_relations(one)
relations[c("A", "B", "C"), c("A", "B", "C")]
```

`get_grades()` returns an integer vector named by `entity_id`.
`get_relations()` returns an `n x n` integer matrix in which entry `[i, j]` is
`1` when row entity `i` is placed in a higher-priority grade than column
entity `j`, `-1` for the opposite order, and `0` when the pair shares a grade
(or on the diagonal). Thus `[ "A", "B" ]` is `0` (left unordered) and
`[ "A", "C" ]` is `1` (`A` ordered above `C`).

```{r a6-profile}
profile <- get_profile(one)
knitr::kable(profile[, c("criterion", "weight", "E", "E_over_M",
  "E_over_N", "risk")], digits = 5, row.names = FALSE)
risk <- get_risk(one)
risk
```

In `get_profile()`, `E` is the posterior expected number of wrong-direction
ordered pairs on that criterion, `E_over_N` divides `E` by the number of
ordered pairs `N`, `E_over_M` divides `E` by all `M` pairs, and `risk` adds
the unordered-pair cost `tau * (M - N) / M`:

```{r a6-loss}
N <- sum(relations[upper.tri(relations)] != 0L)
M <- choose(length(grades), 2)
tau <- 0.2
c(from_parts = (profile$E + tau * (M - N)) / M, stored = risk$risk)
```

With multiple criteria, `get_profile(two)` has one row per criterion, while
`get_risk(two)` returns a named list (`risk`, `lower_bound`, `gap`, and
`status`) for the overall objective (weighted average of criterion losses by
default, or worst-criterion loss when `objective = "minimax"`).

You can also evaluate any fixed integer grade vector on the same input without
running a solver via `postrank_evaluate()`. Placing every site in grade 1
leaves all pairs unordered:

```{r a6-all-withheld}
withheld <- postrank_evaluate(
  setNames(rep(1L, length(grades)), names(grades)), sites$one,
  weights = c(score_A = 1), tau = 0.2
)
withheld[c("N", "E_over_N", "primary_risk")]
```

Because `N` is `0`, `E_over_N` is `NA` (not `0`) and `primary_risk` equals
`tau` (`0.2`). That all-unordered report is a valid one-grade action, which is
distinct from a failed or timed-out solver run that returned no checked
grading.

## Solver status, bounds, and missing-grade states {#keep-computation-status-with-the-numbers}

Both stored tutorial results have status `"optimal"`. On larger problems or
tight time limits, a solver run can stop before proving optimality or before
finding any checked grading. Always read the status alongside whether a
checked grading is present (`!is.null(get_grades(x))`):

| Solver status and grading state | How to read it |
|:--|:--|
| `"optimal"`, with a checked grading | Optimal within the requested solver tolerances; check `lower_bound`, `gap`, and `warnings` for the numerical details. |
| `"feasible_not_certified"`, with a checked grading | A valid grading was found and checked, while the lower bound or gap did not reach the requested optimality tolerance. |
| `"time_limit"`, with a checked grading | Search stopped at the time limit; the stored best grading can be used and reported together with its remaining `gap` (or `NA` if no bound was obtained). |
| `"time_limit"`, without a checked grading | Search stopped before any candidate grading passed validation; there are no grades to use, though `status` and any `lower_bound` remain recorded. |
| `"infeasible"` | The requested constraints (for example, tight criterion error budgets `q` or `exact_G`) cannot be satisfied simultaneously; this is not an all-unordered grading. |

Statuses `"numerical_error"`, `"unknown"`, or `"unbounded"` indicate solver
trouble; inspect the recorded `warnings` before using any output. As explained
in [Computing grades, choosing settings, and reading solver bounds](m5-computing-grades.html),
the optimization `gap` measures how close the returned grading's loss is to
the solver's lower bound for the supplied comparison probabilities, not
posterior uncertainty in the entity scores.

When a run finishes without a checked grading, `get_grades()` and
`get_relations()` return `NULL`, `as.data.frame()` and `get_profile()` return
zero-row data frames with their normal column names and types, and `get_risk()`
keeps `status` and any `lower_bound` while setting `risk` and `gap` to `NA`.
Never substitute `rep(1L, n)` for `NULL` grades: `NULL` means no checked
grading was returned.

## Saving CSV tables and RDS objects {#save-a-table-and-preserve-an-analysis}

Use CSV when exporting flat tables to other software, and RDS when saving the
complete `postrank_analysis` object in R with its settings, report card,
solver bounds, and warnings intact. Here we write both to a fresh temporary
folder:

```{r a6-export-folder}
export_dir <- tempfile("postrank-exports-")
dir.create(export_dir)
csv_file <- file.path(export_dir, "grades.csv")
rds_file <- file.path(export_dir, "analysis.rds")
```

```{r a6-csv}
write.csv(grade_table, csv_file, row.names = FALSE)
csv_again <- read.csv(csv_file,
  colClasses = c(entity_id = "character", grade = "integer"))
identical(csv_again, grade_table)
```

Specify `colClasses = c(entity_id = "character", grade = "integer")` when
reading CSV files back into R so leading zeros in IDs such as `"01001"` are
preserved, and `row.names = FALSE` when writing so no extra row-number column
is added. Because a CSV table drops policy settings, interval levels, and
solver status, record those alongside any exported table.

```{r a6-rds}
saveRDS(one, rds_file)
restored <- readRDS(rds_file)
identical(get_grades(restored), grades)
identical(get_risk(restored), risk)
identical(as.data.frame(restored, what = "report_card"), card)
```

`readRDS()` restores the full analysis object without calling a solver. Keep
the `postrank` version and source input alongside archived `.rds` files for
long-term reproducibility.

## Writing a standalone HTML report {#write-a-standalone-html-report}

`postrank_report()` writes a self-contained English HTML report from stored
results without running a solver. Note that its first argument must be the
`postrank_fit` object (`one$fit`, not `one` directly), while passing
`analysis = one` supplies the report card and any stored optional summaries
(matching diagnostics stored on `analysis` or passed via `diagnostics =`,
including `postrank_coefficient_diagnose()` summaries and their `NA_reason`
fields, are included when present; missing summaries stay marked unavailable and
are never recomputed):

```{r report-example}
html_file <- file.path(export_dir, "grades-report.html")
report <- postrank_report(one$fit, analysis = one,
  output_file = html_file, lang = "en")
report
basename(report$output_file)
```

Line 1 of `print(report)` (`Report saved as grades-report.html`) confirms that
the file was written to `output_file` (the generic footer line mentioning
`output_file` is always printed by `postrank_report`'s console formatter).
Figures are embedded directly in the HTML file for offline viewing; set
`figures = FALSE` for a smaller text-and-table report. `postrank_report()`
refuses to overwrite an existing `output_file`, so choose a new file path for
each saved report version, and write to a project directory rather than
`tempfile()` when keeping reports across R sessions.
